$comment: The pack manifest (ENT-233). It is the list of what the corpus contains and
the order it must be ingested in, held as data so that adding a regulation is
an edit here rather than an edit to Go.
Before this file, `corpuspack.All` carried `[]string{GDPRFile, AIActFile}` and
two consts naming those files. A third regulation meant a code change, a
release, and a drift test that counted packs. That is the shape ENT-233 exists
to remove: a pack is data the harness loads, not a shape the harness is built
around.
ORDER IS LOAD-BEARING, NOT COSMETIC. Obligations cite articles, and the
citation check reads the database rather than the pack, so every regulation a
pack of obligations cites has to be ingested before it. A run that sent
obligations first would have every one of them refused against an empty
corpus, entirely correctly. The loader preserves this order and does not sort.
`kind` selects the parser, because the five files have four different shapes
and the curator's JSON is hand-edited rather than generated. `id` names the
pack in logs and in the ingest response; nothing is stored under it, and the
natural keys inside the pack (CELEX, slug) are what the corpus is addressed
by. A pack renamed is not a new corpus.

packs.title: Derived compliance obligations
$comment: One file spanning both regulations, which is a known seam rather than an
oversight: an obligation is keyed to the law it cites, so its pack
membership is `citation.celex` and not the file it happens to live in.
Splitting it per regulation is deferred until a third act makes the
shared file genuinely awkward. docs/regulation-packs.md has the
reasoning and the cost.
